items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we'll describe a procedure known as borrowing. Borrowing is used often when subtracting large numbers, as we'll soon discover.

Content:
Let's consider the place value chart of the number [MATH: 30\mathbin{:}]

Content:
| tens | ones |
| [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 0] |

Content:
Since [MATH: 3 \, \textrm{tens} = {\color{red}{2}} \, \textrm{tens} + {\color{blue}{1}} \, \textrm{tens},] we can write our place value chart as follows:

Content:
| tens | ones |
| [MATH: {\color{red}2}+{\color{blue}1}] | [MATH: 0] |

Content:
Now, since [MATH: 1] ten is the same as [MATH: 10] ones, we can borrow [MATH: {\color{blue}1}] from tens place and convert it into ones:

Content:
| tens | ones |
| [MATH: {\color{red}2}+{\color{blue}1}] | [MATH: 0] |
| [MATH: {\color{blue} 10 \, \textrm{ones} \rightarrow}] |

Content:
Therefore, we have now have [MATH: \color{red}2] tens and [MATH: {\color{blue}{10}}\,\textrm{ones} + 0\,\textrm{ones} = {\color{blue}{10}}\,\textrm{ones}.]

Content:
| tens | ones |
| [MATH: \color{red}2] | [MATH: {\color{blue}10}] |

Content:
Therefore, "[MATH: 3] tens" is equivalent to "[MATH: 2] tens and [MATH: 10] ones."
